In July, Sierra Sharry and Lane Smith were expecting a baby. Sharry was eight months pregnant when Smith fell and hit his head. He was taken to a hospital in Oklahoma City, but he never recovered. Sharry said on Facebook that July 13, 2014, was the worst day of her life because she lost her best friend and the father of her unborn child. Their son, Taos, was born a few weeks later. When it was time for his six-month photos, Sharry asked the photographer to make the family look complete in just one picture.

People have different opinions about Indiana’s new religious freedom law. Some people are angry because they believe the law allows businesses to treat gay and lesbian customers unfairly by using religion as an excuse. Others, like Indiana Governor Mike Pence, are surprised by the criticism. He argues that the law is similar to laws that already exist in the federal government and 19 other states. The debate is intense because people disagree on what the law means and why it was created.

Some fans of Lucille Ball want a statue of her removed from a park in her hometown, Celoron, New York. They say the statue looks ugly and does not look like the famous "I Love Lucy" star. People have compared the life-size bronze statue to singer Conway Twitty, the snake from the movie "Beetlejuice," and actor Steve Buscemi. Even the mayor, Scott Schrecengost, says he does not like the statue, which shows Lucille Ball holding a bottle of a fictional drink called Vitameatavegamin. However, the statue has been a popular attraction for tourists since 2009, drawing visitors who take photos with it.

Muhammadu Buhari became Nigeria’s leader this time through voting, not by force. This election is very important for five reasons. First, it is the first time in Nigeria’s history that the opposition party won against the ruling party in a fair election. Buhari, who is 72 years old, won the presidential election by beating the current leader, Goodluck Jonathan, by about two million votes. Nigeria is important because it is Africa’s largest economy, its most populous country, and one of its biggest oil producers. It also sends a lot of crude oil to the United States.

People in Iran were celebrating very loudly, both online and in the streets. It felt like they had just won the World Cup, but this event was even more important. Young people waved flags from their car sunroofs, played music loudly, and talked on the internet using the hashtag #IranTalks. This excitement happened because Iran reached a major agreement with the United States and other countries about its nuclear program. This deal is expected to end Iran’s isolation and remove the strict economic penalties that have been in place for years. Just before midnight on Thursday, Vali Asr street, a main road in Tehran, became like a street party. Car horns were honking, men were dancing in the traffic, and some people showed off U.S. dollar bills.

A court in Brooklyn has charged a fourth man, Dilkhayot Kasimov, with helping terrorists and joining ISIS. He was added to a new legal document that also charges three other men: Abdurasul Hasanovich Juraboev, Akhror Saidakhmetov, and Abror Habibov. These three men are accused of supporting a foreign terrorist group and have said they are not guilty. It is not clear whether Kasimov has been arrested yet.

On Saturday, North America saw the third part of a four-part lunar eclipse series. This was the shortest eclipse in the group, but it was still enjoyable for people who woke up early. The moon went completely into Earth’s shadow at 4:58 a.m. Pacific Time (7:58 a.m. Eastern Time). This total eclipse lasted for nearly five minutes. NASA says this is the shortest total lunar eclipse of the century. Before, during, and after the eclipse, the moon looked burnt-orange. This color is why total lunar eclipses are called "blood moons."

Istanbul, Turkey (CNN) – On Tuesday, people in Turkey were worried and confused. An older woman wearing a white headscarf and carrying shopping bags stood outside a closed subway entrance. She asked, "What is happening? Why can't I enter the subway?" She was part of millions of people affected by the biggest power outage in Turkey in over ten years. For several hours, many cities across the country lost electricity. Millions of people were impacted, including passengers stuck in trains and subways that stopped working.

During Holy Week, we should remember what the Bible says about fair wages. Isaiah 58:6 describes a true fast as breaking injustice, stopping workplace exploitation, freeing oppressed people, and canceling debts.

McDonald’s decision to raise wages for 90,000 employees is a big win for fast-food workers and their supporters. By standing together, these workers are making it harder for profitable companies like McDonald’s to pay such low wages that keep workers in poverty.

California is facing a severe drought, and Governor Jerry Brown has ordered everyone—residents, businesses, and farms—to cut their water use by 25%. This is the first time mandatory water restrictions have been imposed in the state. Brown stated that the era of watering lawns daily is over. This 25% reduction will save about 1.5 million acre-feet of water over the next nine months. One acre-foot of water is roughly equal to 325,000 gallons.

In London, UK voters have very little time left to choose their candidates. Polling stations are about to open across the country for an election that might significantly change the political situation. This campaign has been very short, especially compared to U.S. elections, where candidates often spend years refining their messages. The election could result in power shifting from David Cameron’s Conservative government to the Labour Party, led by Ed Miliband. Alternatively, political leaders might struggle to form alliances with smaller parties. However, these outcomes will only be known when the polls close late Thursday evening, local time.

This is the time of year when Christians around the world—more than 2 billion people—think about the death and resurrection of Jesus. Because of the recent killing of Christian students in Kenya and the ongoing danger to Christians in other countries, we are asking Christians this Holy Week to also remember the many ways their faith has made them targets of religious extremists. These dangers include being crucified, beheaded, stoned, forced into slavery, sexually abused, trafficked, harassed, bombed, and forced to leave their homes.

The racist and offensive emails that caused three employees in Ferguson, Missouri, to quit or lose their jobs have been made public. These messages were between the city’s top court clerk and two police officers. They were found during a U.S. Justice Department investigation into racial bias in the city’s police and court systems. The emails contain offensive comments about President Barack Obama, First Lady Michelle Obama, Muslims, and minorities. The Washington Post got the emails on Thursday after asking for them through a public records request. CNN looked at them on Friday. Police Captain Rick Henke and Sergeant...

Two people were arrested in Australia after police found at least 55 dead dogs dumped in the bush in Queensland. One of the arrested people is a licensed greyhound trainer. The two people are a 71-year-old man and a 64-year-old woman from Bundaberg. They were charged with illegally possessing a gun. The woman was also charged with blocking police officers. The RSPCA, an animal rights group, is helping the police investigate the case.

Two years ago, Mike Premeau and Kathy Danke started a small business called Memories Gourmet Pizza Co. in their town in Wisconsin. They were successful, selling frozen pizzas—including breakfast and gluten-free options—in stores across Nichols, an area west of Green Bay. They also built a loyal customer base.

However, this week, their business was threatened because people confused them with Memories Pizza of Walkerton, Indiana. That other business made national news after its owners said they would not cater a same-sex wedding. As a result, angry people posted comments on Memories Gourmet Pizza’s Facebook page and called their phone number to protest.

Archaeologists from the University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna found a complete camel skeleton under a cellar in Austria. The bones were discovered in 2006 and 2007 while workers were building a shopping center in the city of Tulln. Experts believe this camel was used by Ottoman soldiers who attacked Vienna in the 17th century. At first, researchers thought the bones belonged to a large horse or cow. However, an expert named Alfred Galik identified the animal as a camel by looking at its neck bones, lower jaw, and hand bones.

Andrew Getty, 47, died on Tuesday afternoon at his home in Los Angeles. His parents, Ann and Gordon Getty, announced the news and asked the media and public to respect the family’s privacy during this difficult time. The Los Angeles County coroner’s office said the death was likely due to natural causes or an accident. Investigators found some medication at the house, but they do not know if Andrew was taking it or what his medical history was.

We may never fully understand why co-pilot Andreas Lubitz crashed Germanwings Flight 9525 into the French Alps on March 24, killing everyone on the plane. A new report shows that he made the plane descend faster, leading to the crash. This is very frightening. As the investigation continues, we will find out more about how much Lubitz hid his mental illness, how much help he asked for, and how his depression affected his ability to fly. Should he have quit his job? Should his doctors have warned others? His case highlights important questions about people with mental illness and the shame they often feel.

On April 8, 2015, CNN Student News covered several stories. First, it discussed news about the United States and Cuba. Then, it explained how California’s serious drought is affecting other parts of the country. The program also mentioned a flu outbreak in Chicago, but clarified that it does not affect humans. Finally, it talked about a plan to build a tunnel connecting Denmark and Germany, which would include roads and train tracks under the sea. On this page, you can find the transcript of today’s show and a way to ask to be included in the CNN Student News Roll Call. Click here to read the transcript.

A man who refused to give his name was identified by a tattoo on his neck that said "Gertrude." This is what Kankakee County, Illinois, Sheriff Tim Bukowski said on Saturday about Kamron Taylor. Taylor is a 23-year-old man who was convicted of murder but escaped from jail before being arrested in Chicago overnight.

Police in Illinois had been searching for Taylor since early Wednesday. On that day, he jumped a correctional officer at the Jerome Combs Detention Center in Kankakee. He then fled with the officer’s uniform and an SUV.

Surveillance video was the last thing officials saw of Taylor until just before midnight on Friday, when he appeared in Chicago. "They saw a guy that matched the description," Bukowski said.

Prince Harry, who is 30 years old, is finishing his military career in Britain. He will spend time in Australia, arriving on Monday for a four-week period. During this time, he will work and live with Australian soldiers in Sydney, Darwin, and Perth. A spokesman for the Australian military said that Harry has already worked with Australian troops several times during his 10 years in the military.

Two Florida prison guards and one former guard trainee have been charged with trying to kill a former prisoner who was about to be released. The Florida Attorney General announced this on Thursday.

An FBI informant met these three men—Thomas Jordan Driver, 25; David Elliot Moran, 47; and Charles Thomas Newcomb, 42—after going undercover into a group called the Traditional American Knights of the Ku Klux Klan. According to court documents, Driver told the informant that he had fought with the former inmate and that he and Moran wanted the inmate dead.

On Thursday in Lausanne, Switzerland, a group of world powers called the P5+1 reached a basic agreement with Iran about its nuclear program. It is not yet clear if this agreement will succeed. The parties have until the end of June to work out the details and write the plan down. However, these talks were important, especially because relations between the United States and Iran have been frozen for a long time. The negotiations were not fancy, but they showed how diplomacy can be both very effective and very busy.

On Monday morning, an improvised bomb exploded near a United Nations vehicle in Garowe, a city in northeastern Somalia. The explosion killed six people, including four aid workers from UNICEF, the international children’s agency. Somalia’s President described the event as an attack on the country’s future. This incident happened shortly after a separate attack on Sunday, where three African Union soldiers died in an ambush in the Lower Shabelle region. The terrorist group Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for Monday’s bombing, which took place around 8 a.m. in Garowe, the administrative capital of the Puntland region.

Prince Harry arrived in Australia on Monday. He will spend four weeks working with the Australian military. Before starting his work, the 30-year-old prince visited the Australian War Memorial in Canberra, the capital city. He paid his respects at the Tomb of the Unknown Australian Soldier. A crowd of people gathered outside the memorial. Some took photos of the prince. One boy held a sign that said, "Red Heads Rule!" to celebrate Harry's hair color. During his time in Australia, Harry will work and live with soldiers in Sydney, Darwin, and Perth.

Australia, a key ally of the United States, has agreed to share some intelligence with Iran. Australian Foreign Minister Julie Bishop described the agreement as "informal" and said its main goal is to track Australians who travel to Iraq to fight for ISIS. However, one Australian lawmaker criticized the move, calling it "dancing with the devil." Over the weekend, Bishop became the first Australian government minister to visit Iran in 12 years, meeting with President Hassan Rouhani. The intelligence-sharing deal was announced in an interview released on Monday, which Bishop gave to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation while she was in Tehran.

Tests on the flight data recorder from Germanwings Flight 9525 show that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz intentionally made the plane go down faster. This was reported by the French air accident investigation agency, the BEA. The recorder, often called the "black box," was found on Thursday by teams who had been searching the French Alps for days since the crash on March 24. The BEA said its teams started looking at the recorder's data immediately.

A 110-day chase between a fishing boat and conservationists ended in an unusual way. The conservationists, from a group called Sea Shepherd, were following a boat named the *Thunder*. This boat was wanted by Interpol for suspected fraud and illegal fishing. The chase started in the Southern Ocean when the conservationists' ship, the *Bob Barker*, found the *Thunder*. The chase ended early Monday in the Gulf of Guinea, off the coast of West Africa. The *Bob Barker* received a distress call from the *Thunder*, and the crew of the *Thunder* was rescued by the conservationists.

Most days, 16-year-old Jason Zobott goes to Huntley High School in suburban Chicago around 7:30 a.m., just like other high school students. However, what he does after that is unusual. Zobott is part of a special program at the school that combines online learning with traditional classroom teaching. Currently, one-third of the school’s 2,700 students are in this program. The school plans to enroll most of its students in this program by 2015. Zobott, who is a top student and balances schoolwork with many extracurricular activities, says that working online makes it easier for him to complete his tasks. He adds, “I can learn on my own.”

Days after a terrible attack by the terrorist group Al-Shabaab in Garissa, Kenya, launched airstrikes against the group in Somalia. A military source told CNN that these strikes were not revenge for the massacre at Garissa University College, which killed nearly 150 people last week. The source explained that the attacks on Al-Shabaab bases are part of ongoing military operations that began in 2011, not a response to the recent tragedy. The source spoke on Monday, as is common for Kenyan military officials, who usually do not give their names to the media.

Pope Francis gave his traditional speech after Easter Mass, reminding everyone that the Vatican is a country and that he acts as a moral leader. He spoke about the pain people are suffering in current conflicts and asked for violence to stop everywhere. He specifically called for an end to the fighting in Iraq and Syria and for help to reach people who need it. He said, "May the international community not stand by before the immense humanitarian tragedy unfolding in these countries and the drama of the numerous refugees." This speech, known as "urbi et orbi," is Latin for "to the city (Rome) and to the world."

On Wednesday afternoon, students and staff at Duke University marched together, chanting that they were not afraid and stood united. This happened after a rope noose was found hanging from a tree on campus. The noose was discovered near a student center around 2 a.m. Duke officials have asked anyone who knows about the noose to call campus police. Photos of the noose were shared on social media, causing anger and outrage among the community. Hundreds of people gathered on the steps of Duke Chapel, which is close to where the noose was found, for a forum. One speaker said, "You came here because you want to say with me: This is not the Duke we will accept. This is not the Duke we want. This is not the Duke we are here to experience."

Muhanad Mahmoud Al Farekh, a 29-year-old U.S. citizen, appeared in court in Brooklyn on Thursday. He was charged with helping terrorists, but he did not enter a plea. Al Farekh was sent from Pakistan to the United States. A court document says he planned to fight against American forces in other countries. CNN counterterrorism expert Philip Mudd called this news something to celebrate.

Saudi Arabia reported that a border guard was killed in a gunfight with militants in Yemen this week. This is the first time Saudi Arabia has publicly acknowledged a military death since it started bombing rebels in Yemen.

The fight happened on Wednesday night at the border in southwestern Saudi Arabia. Militants in the mountains of Yemen shot at Saudi border guards, and the guards shot back.

The guard who died was identified as Cpl. Salman Ali Yahya al-Maliki. Ten other people were hurt, but their injuries were not life-threatening.

I was nervous when I went to the Al Marmoum camel race in Dubai. As the only person from the Gulf countries on the CNN team, people expected me to know about camel racing, which is a long-standing tradition in this area. Even though I tried to wear a kandora, which is traditional clothing in the UAE, I still felt like an outsider because my modern way of thinking is different from this world. A friendly farm owner took us into the majlis, which is a meeting space where the camel owners were gathering. The large room looked like a fancy theater. The owners sat on the floor, eating a'aish, a traditional Arabic dish made of fish and rice, which was placed in front of them. The conversation was loud and exciting.

In Havana, Cuba, Charlie Hill sits in a dark bar on a bright, sunny day. He speaks with a rough voice and nods, showing that he knows you have been looking for him. Many people have been searching for Charlie Hill for a long time. For 43 years, Cuba has protected him from charges that he killed a police officer in New Mexico and hijacked an airplane to Havana. Now 65 years old, Hill agreed to speak with CNN after reporters spent two years trying to find him. He wants to talk about how he is now considering leaving his safe place in Cuba and returning to the United States.

On April 2, 2015, CNN Student News covered several topics. First, they explained why Yemen, an unstable country in the Middle East, is becoming a place for a hidden conflict between larger powers. The news also shared the history of April Fools' Day. They reported on how a recipe from 1,000 years ago might help treat a dangerous modern bacteria. Finally, they featured a story about a woman who is helping children improve their lives. You can find the full text of today’s broadcast on this page, and you can also use the page to ask to be included in the CNN Student News Roll Call.

On April 3, 2015, CNN Student News covers stories from Switzerland, Kenya, and the Pacific Ocean. In California, a serious drought is forcing many people and businesses to use less water. The show also talks about two religious holidays celebrated around the world this weekend, and looks at two topics related to U.S. National Parks.

You can find the transcript of today’s show on this page, and you can also request to be part of the CNN Student News Roll Call. Click here to read the transcript.

Misao Okawa, who was recognized by Guinness World Records as the oldest person in the world, has died at age 117. She passed away on Wednesday morning in Osaka, Japan, according to Tadahi Uchimura, a local city official.

Okawa leaves behind three children, four grandchildren, and six great-grandchildren. She was born on March 5, 1898. Her family used to run a kimono shop in Osaka. Satoshi Yoshioka, who works at the nursing home where Okawa has lived since 1997, told CNN that she had a gentle personality and loved to eat. Her favorite foods were sushi and udon noodles. He also noted that she ate a lot of cake for her birthday on March 5 last year

Documents obtained by CNN show that when the Missouri National Guard prepared to go to Ferguson, Missouri, to help stop the protests, they used strong military language. They called the protesters "enemy forces" and "adversaries."

The Guard went to Ferguson to support police officers. However, many community leaders and civil rights activists said the police used too much force and made the tense situation worse. The protests happened sporadically from August through the end of the year.

On Tuesday, gunmen attacked the education ministry building in Mogadishu, Somalia. This happened after a suicide car bomb exploded at the entrance of the building. The attack killed at least 12 people and injured 16 others.

The militant group Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for the attack. A spokesman for the group said they were responsible. A security official said the attack started when two suicide bombers blew up their car at the entrance of the two-story building. Then, five gunmen went inside and shot people.

Gregory Margolin, now 87, fought in World War II as a 16-year-old soldier in the Soviet Red Army. During the war, his family fled, and he hid his Jewish identity because people were being killed everywhere around him. He became a sniper and eventually a commander. Today, in Ukraine, he is facing war again. He still wears his old military uniform with its medals, and his granddaughter, Liora, is amazed that he survived both wars.

It has been exactly one year since more than 200 Nigerian schoolgirls were taken from their dormitory at night in Chibok, northeastern Nigeria. They are still missing. The Nigerian government and the rest of the world have allowed this to happen. We should feel ashamed that young girls’ lives can be destroyed by violent criminals without punishment. We should also feel ashamed that people quickly forget about such terrible events.

In Norway, digital technology is replacing FM radio. The country plans to stop using FM radio completely within two years, making it the first nation in the world to do so. This change does not mean people will lose access to radio; they will just listen to it digitally instead. Officials in Oslo say that many of the country’s 5 million people have already switched. On traditional FM radio, there are only five stations available. However, on the Digital Audio Broadcasting network, there are four times as many stations. According to Culture Minister Thorhild Widvey, half of the country already listens to radio digitally.

Everyone enjoys a good comeback story, especially one involving dinosaurs. For over 100 years, the Brontosaurus was removed from science books, but a new study suggests it should have its own name. The Brontosaurus belongs to its own group of dinosaurs, so it deserves to be called by its original name. In 1879, O.C. Marsh named the Brontosaurus after receiving 25 crates of bones found at Como Bluff in Wyoming, according to the Yale Peabody Museum of Natural History. The dinosaur was similar to, but not as large as, the Apatosaurus, which had been discovered a few years earlier. Marsh named it "Brontosaurus," which means "thunder lizard."

Al Qaeda in Yemen has announced a reward of 20 kilograms of gold for anyone who kills or captures two key Shia Muslim leaders. This includes Abdelmalik Bedrudin Al-Houthi, the rebel leader who took control of Yemen’s capital, and former President Ali Abdullah Saleh. The gold is worth about $774,000. Al Qaeda calls these two men the “two heads of evil.” Al Qaeda is one of several groups fighting to control Yemen.

Before landing his gyrocopter on the Capitol lawn on Wednesday, Doug Hughes explained his plans and reasons on a website called thedemocracyclub.org. The 61-year-old Florida postal worker wrote in an online post titled "Your Pilot" that his goal was to highlight corruption in Washington, D.C., and to offer solutions to that problem. He stated that his flight was not a secret. Before taking off, he sent an email to info@barackobama.com. The letter was meant to convince Capitol officials that he was not a threat, and that shooting him down would cause more trouble than letting him deliver letters to Congress.

Rio de Janeiro is facing more problems before the 2016 Olympics. Many dead fish were found in the Rodrigo de Freitas lagoon. The Games' rowing and canoe events will take place in the city in just over a year. On Monday, officials from Rio’s legislative assembly started an investigation to find out why the fish died. They will look at the lagoon and other lakes and bays in the state where this has happened. The investigation team will work with the State Environmental Institute (INEA) and the State Secretariat for the Environment.

Anthony Ray Hinton is 58 years old, but he is new to the outside world. He spent nearly 30 years on death row in Alabama. Because of this, simple things like using a fork, going out at night, or sleeping without someone checking on him feel strange to him.

One week ago, his murder convictions were canceled, and he was released from a county jail in Birmingham. He told CNN’s Brooke Baldwin that he has to pinch himself to believe he is free. He said it will take some time to get used to being free.

For 30 years, Hinton spent most of his time locked in a small cell that was only 5 feet by 7 feet.

After the UK election debate, the polls showed that there was no clear winner. The debate featured seven party leaders: David Cameron (Conservatives), Ed Miliband (Labour), Nick Clegg (Liberal Democrats), Nigel Farage (UK Independence Party), Natalie Bennett (Green Party), Nicola Sturgeon (Scottish National Party), and Leanne Wood (Plaid Cymru, the Welsh Nationalists).

Two different polling companies gave slightly different results, but they all agreed that the top performers were close. Comres, which organized the debate for ITV, found that Cameron, Miliband, and Farage were tied for first place with 21% each, while Sturgeon was close behind with 20%.
